Hook: New Year's Eve, 2014, in New York: one of the busiest nights of the year for a ride-hailing app. When requests outrun the drivers on the road, the app raises the fare, the surge, until the two match. That night a fault switched surge pricing off for twenty-six minutes. Fares stayed at the normal price. Requests piled up, drivers did not come, and riders opening the app saw no cars. During the outage only about a quarter of requests were completed. After a sold-out concert at Madison Square Garden, with surge working, nearly every request had been met. The comparison comes from a case study by the company's own economists, which is itself part of this part's story: firms now employ economists to design their markets, run their experiments and measure what their prices do.

The Island has a ride-hailing app too, and a New Year's Eve. At the normal fare, requests spike at midnight to more than five times the usual rate. With surge off, the drivers on the road stay at their usual number, and everything above that line goes unfilled: at the peak, about 27 percent of requests are completed. With surge on, the fare rises, to 2.8 times normal at the peak. Some riders wait, walk or share instead, while more drivers come out, a few minutes later. Every request that is made is filled. Who gains and who loses is the subject of chapter three; here, the point is what a price does when it is allowed to move.

The question: what do the economists inside technology companies do? They help set a platform's prices, fees and rules. They study what ranking, ratings and ad auctions do to the market. They ask whether advertising pays, and how anyone could know. They design experiments in markets where every buyer shares the same drivers or rooms. And they ask what a free service is worth to the people who use it.
Economics, Built. Part sixty-one: economics at the platforms.

Part sixty set one firm's prices. This part runs a marketplace. By the end you will know how a platform is designed, from its commission and surge pricing to its ranking and ratings; how ad auctions work in practice, and why the return on advertising is so hard to measure; how experiments are run at scale, and what goes wrong when units interfere; how machine learning is used to target and to forecast long-term effects; and what flexible work and free services are worth to the people who use them.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: set the commission.

Your turn. You run the Island's ride-hailing app, and you choose one number: the commission, the share of each fare the platform keeps. The fare is twenty dollars a trip, and here it is fixed. Drivers drive when their pay for an hour beats their other work, about twenty dollars an hour; riders ride when the wait is short, and the wait grows as drivers get busy. So the commission works through both sides: a higher commission means lower pay per trip, fewer drivers, longer waits, and fewer riders. Ten percent, twenty, thirty, or forty-five: which earns the platform the most?

Here is each commission's equilibrium, where the drivers who choose to drive and the riders who choose to ride are consistent with each other's choices. At ten percent, 176 trips an hour, but the platform keeps only 352 dollars. At twenty, 562. At thirty, 622, the most of the four, from 104 trips. At forty-five percent the take falls back, to 479: drivers' pay is so low that only 47 drive, waits stretch to 6 minutes, and riders give up. So C. The platform's best commission on a fine grid is 29 percent. Below it, trips are many but too little is kept from each; above it, there are too few drivers and too long a wait.

Now look at everyone, not just the platform. Riders' surplus, in dollars an hour, drivers' surplus, and the platform's take, peaking at 29 percent. Moving from ten percent to thirty, the platform gains 270 dollars an hour, and riders and drivers together lose 1,270. The loss is so much larger because of a cross-side effect: each driver who stops driving lengthens every rider's wait, and the commission, chosen for the platform's take alone, ignores it. This is Part forty-four's two-sided market with numbers in it. What keeps commissions down in practice is competition: between platforms, and from drivers and riders who keep two apps on their phones.
Surge: Surge pricing is the oldest idea in this series: a price that clears the market. Take the Island's peak minute. Riders' requests fall as the fare rises, and the number of drivers on the road rises with it. At the normal fare, 340 requests meet 70 drivers, and the shortage is rationed by luck and by waiting. The fare that clears the market is 2.1 times normal. At that fare there are 121 rides a minute, not 70: more rides, not fewer, because the higher fare brings out drivers who would otherwise have stayed at home. The app's own multiplier runs above the static answer for the first minutes of a spike, because drivers take time to arrive; surge is a price that has to anticipate its own supply.

Surge also does something for the economist: it varies the price, many times a day, for reasons riders cannot see. Here are the Island's riders who opened the app when the surge happened to be at each level, and the share who booked. Those points trace out the demand curve. The area under it, above the fare, is what riders would have paid and did not have to: consumer surplus. On the Island it comes to 1.42 dollars for every dollar spent. Cohen, Hahn, Hall, Levitt and Metcalfe did this with almost fifty million sessions in four American cities in 2015. They found demand inelastic, with elasticities mostly between minus 0.4 and minus 0.6, and about a dollar sixty of consumer surplus for every dollar spent. Their variation came from the surge algorithm's rounding: sessions just above and just below a threshold saw different prices for the same conditions, a regression discontinuity. Two of the authors worked for the company, which supplied the data; the design is what makes the number worth taking seriously.

So who gains? Riders who would pay more get a car; drivers earn more on the busiest nights; riders who would not pay the higher fare are priced out, where without surge they would have waited, mostly in vain. And yet surge is widely hated. A price that jumps when you most need the service feels like exploitation; Part forty-five's fairness norms are real constraints on what firms can charge. In July 2014 the company agreed with New York's attorney general that in emergencies, from storms to power failures, fares would be capped at the range of the previous sixty days, leaving out the three highest days. And surge cannot conjure drivers who are too far away to arrive in time: in the first minutes of a spike, a higher fare only decides which riders get the cars already on the road.
Ranking: Every marketplace is also a search engine, and its first design decision is the order of the results. Here are the Island marketplace's logged clicks on each position of a results page. The top result gets 5.1 times as many clicks as the fifth. But that mixes two things: the top result is at the top, and it is also the result the algorithm thought most relevant. What the platform needs to know is the effect of position alone: the chance that a shopper looks at each slot at all. On the Island, position alone gives the top slot 3.3 times the fifth's attention; the rest of the logged gap is relevance. Platforms learn this by randomizing the order for a small share of searches. Raluca Ursu did it with a travel site's hotel rankings, randomized: position changed which hotels people looked at, and much less which they booked once they had looked.

Now sell the top of the page. Here is the page in order of relevance, the best the shopper could see. A seller whose listing is sixth by relevance pays for the top slot, and the two listings swap. Shoppers now look first at a worse match: clicks per search fall from 2.05 to 1.84, and the relevance of what they click falls from 0.597 to 0.538. The platform earns the ad's price, and pays for it in its shoppers' attention and trust. How many sponsored slots, and how far up, is a trade-off the platform's economists measure with experiments, because the cost shows up only slowly, in shoppers who come back less.

And when the platform that ranks also sells? It can put its own products first. That was Part forty-four's worry about vertical integration; here it becomes a question of measurement. In 2017 the European Commission fined Google two point four two billion euros for favouring its own comparison shopping service in its search results, a decision the EU's Court of Justice upheld in 2024. The economist's job in such a case is to measure how much of the ranking is relevance and how much is ownership, and what shoppers lose by it. And the remedy has a problem of its own: a rule against favouring yourself needs a definition of the neutral ranking, and there is no such thing, since every ranking is a choice about what shoppers should see first.
Reputation: Ratings let strangers trust each other, and they have a famous problem: almost everyone is excellent. The Island's marketplace has two thousand sellers, each delivering a good transaction between eighty and ninety-nine percent of the time. Happy buyers leave a positive rating sixty percent of the time; unhappy ones mostly say nothing, and complain only five percent of the time. So the score the platform displays, positive ratings over all ratings, piles up at the top: a median of 99.1 percent, with 84 percent of sellers at ninety-eight or more. Chris Nosko and Steven Tadelis proposed counting the silence: positive ratings over all transactions, the effective percent positive. It spreads the sellers out. And it tracks their true quality better, a correlation of 0.68 against 0.51. On eBay they found the displayed score had a median of one hundred percent and a mean of 99.3, while the effective score had a median of 67 percent. Their argument: a bad transaction hurts not only the seller but the platform, because a buyer who had one is less likely to come back at all.

What can a platform do? First see why ratings inflate: unhappy buyers stay silent, a bad review invites a bad one back, and raters feel sorry for the person they are rating. In 2014 Airbnb ran an experiment that hid each review until both guest and host had written theirs, so neither could retaliate. Andrey Fradkin, Elena Grewal and David Holtz found fewer retaliating and reciprocating reviews, slightly lower ratings, and more reviews written; the design was then given to everyone. Second, count what is unsaid: silence, returns, complaints and whether a buyer ever comes back. Underneath is Part fifteen's logic: a rating is a public good. Each rater helps strangers, not themselves, so ratings are undersupplied and shaded, and the platform, which gains from trust, has to supply the system that produces it.
AdAuctions: Chapter six. Ad auctions in practice.

Part sixteen built the generalized second-price auction for search ads. Here is the piece it left for the practitioners: quality. Four advertisers bid for three slots. Ranked by bid alone, A, the highest bidder, takes the top slot. But A's ad is a poor match for the search: searchers click it half as often as an average ad. Its quality score is a half. Rank by bid times quality instead, the expected payment per search, and B takes the top slot, A drops to second. Each advertiser pays the least it could have bid and kept its slot: the next advertiser's score divided by its own quality. A, with the worse ad, pays more per click than B. Searchers click more, 0.46 times a search against 0.40, and the platform earns more too, 1.005 dollars a search against 0.970: quality scores align the platform's revenue with its users' interest. A reserve price of a dollar fifty lifts the last slot's price and the revenue to 1.020, Part sixteen's Myerson reserve at work.

The design keeps changing. In 2008 Yahoo! let Michael Ostrovsky and Michael Schwarz set reserve prices by Myerson's rule on hundreds of thousands of keywords, with others held back as controls. Revenue rose on busy keywords and fell on rare ones, where reserves drove bidders away: a few percent overall, which at that scale is a great deal of money. That dial returns at the end of this part. In 2019 Google moved its display-ad exchange to first-price auctions; bidders spread across many exchanges were already shading their bids, and the second price had lost its simplicity. Today most advertisers do not bid at all: they give the platform a budget and a target cost, and its algorithm bids for them, so the bidders in the auction are the platform's own software, a design problem Part sixteen's theory is still catching up with. The economist's work is to set reserves, quality formulas and formats, and to test each change on a slice of the traffic before it goes everywhere.
AdWork: The Island's marketplace buys ads on a search engine, and its dashboard says they pay twelve times over. Here is the truth the Island knows. 40 percent of the people searching for it are regulars, who buy thirty percent of the time, ad or no ad. The rest buy two percent of the time, and seeing the ad raises that by three tenths of a point. When the ad is there, half of all searchers click it, at fifty cents a click; when it is not, they click the free link just below. The dashboard counts every sale that came through an ad click, about 67 per thousand searchers, most of them regulars. The ads caused 1.8. So the dashboard reports a return of 1,238 percent. A regression of sales on ad spending across regions and weeks does no better: 2,607 percent, because spending rises with searches, and searches rise with the people who were going to buy anyway. The true return is minus 64 percent: every dollar of ads brings back 0.36.

How would the marketplace find out? By switching the ads off. In a random 30 percent of its 210 regions, the ads stop for eight weeks. Compare the change in sales per searcher where the ads stopped with the change where they kept running: a difference in differences. Each dot is one run of that experiment, with the Island's ordinary noise in weekly sales. They scatter, by about 32 points either way, around the truth, minus 64 percent. The experiment is noisy, but it is centred on the right answer; the dashboard and the regression were precise, and wrong by a factor of thirty or more.

The Island's numbers were planted to echo a real experiment. eBay's economists Thomas Blake and Chris Nosko, with Steven Tadelis, persuaded the company to switch its search ads off. First the ads on searches for eBay itself: when they stopped, ninety-nine and a half percent of the clicks still arrived, through the free link underneath. Then all other keywords, switched off for sixty days in regions holding thirty percent of eBay's American traffic. The estimated return was minus sixty-three percent, with a confidence interval from minus a hundred and twenty-four to minus three. The same data, analysed the usual way, with a regression of sales on ad spending, gave returns of over fourteen hundred percent. The ads did move new and occasional buyers; but the frequent buyers, who made most of the sales the ads were credited with, would have bought anyway.

Why don't firms just run the experiment? Because the arithmetic is brutal. Randall Lewis and Justin Rao called it the unfavourable economics of measuring the returns to advertising. Suppose a campaign spends ten cents a person, and returns twenty-five percent: twelve and a half cents of extra sales per person. But what one person spends is wildly variable: here an average of seven dollars, with a standard deviation of seventy-five. The effect is 0.17 percent of one person's noise. To detect that the campaign does anything at all takes 5.7 million people in each arm. To tell a twenty-five percent return from breaking even takes 141 million. Only the largest advertisers, on the largest platforms, can learn whether their advertising pays; everyone else is guessing, and the dashboards guess high.

Called it? Blake, Nosko and Tadelis quoted the advice Google gave its advertisers: determining your return can be a very straightforward process. Take the revenue from sales made via your ads, subtract their cost, and divide by the cost. eBay's experiment found that the same calculation, which gave thousands of percent, missed the sign: the true return on non-brand ads was negative. The verdict: wrong. The sales that come through an ad are not the sales the ad causes. That sentence is most of what economists brought to advertising.
Experiments: Large platforms run thousands of experiments a year, and the first thing that goes wrong is impatience. Here are A/A tests on the Island: both arms see exactly the same page, two thousand users a day each, so there is nothing to find. The grey band is where the difference is not significant at five percent. Read each test once, at the end of thirty days, and 5 percent cross the line, as they should. But a dashboard that updates every morning invites a peek, and a test stopped at the first significant day declares a winner 27 percent of the time. Red lines are the tests that would have shipped a change that does nothing. The fixes are old: decide the length in advance, or use tests whose error rate holds at every look, the sequential methods of Statistics, Built.

The second problem is noise, and the cheapest fix is information the platform already has. What a user spends during a test is predictable from what the same user spent before it. Subtract the part of the difference that the pre-period predicts, and the estimate keeps its centre but loses much of its noise. Microsoft's experimenters called this CUPED; it is the regression adjustment of Part four and of Statistics, Built, applied at scale. Across a thousand Island tests of twenty thousand users, the plain difference in means spreads like the grey curve; adjusted, like the pink one. The variance falls to 0.54 of the plain estimator's; theory says one minus the squared correlation, 0.51. The same precision with about half the users: for a platform, that means twice as many experiments a year.

Experimentation platforms grow habits. Check the split: if the arms are not the sizes the design promised, something in the pipeline broke, and every number from the test is suspect. Watch the guardrails: every test also tracks what it must not hurt, like page speed, complaints and cancellations. Expect novelty: a new design draws clicks because it is new, and an effect measured in a week can fade, or grow, over months, which is chapter ten's problem. And distrust the spectacular: a large, surprising win is more often a bug than a breakthrough. Ron Kohavi, who led experimentation at Microsoft, made that a rule, under the name of Twyman's law.
Interference: Part sixty's hotel rooms come back as drivers. The Island tests a twenty percent discount for riders. In each city, about 170 drivers an hour serve riders of whom 150 want a ride at the normal fare; the discount raises that to 210, more than there are drivers. Design one, the ordinary A/B test: in every city and every hour, half the riders get the discount. But the discounted riders request more, and the drivers they take are drivers the other riders would have had. The control group is not what the world would look like without the discount; it is worse. Design two, the switchback: whole city-hours get the discount or not, at random, so within any hour everyone shares the same treatment. Design three: whole cities, for the whole test.

Here is what each design reports, averaged over four hundred runs, against the truth: the extra rides per hundred riders if everyone got the discount. The A/B test by user says 18.0 more rides per hundred riders, 2.7 times the truth, because most of the discounted riders' extra rides were taken from the control riders, not created. The switchback finds 6.7, give or take 0.7, and the city test 6.8, give or take 4.5: centred on the truth, 6.7, but noisier, since twenty cities are only twenty units. That is the trade: a clean comparison costs units. Switchbacks have their own catch: hours must be long enough for drivers to settle, or one hour's discount leaks into the next through where the drivers are. Platforms now also randomize both sides at once, riders and drivers or buyers and listings separately, and compare the four cells to see the interference itself: two-sided randomization, studied by Ramesh Johari and colleagues and by Patrick Bajari and colleagues at Amazon.
CausalML: Chapter ten. Causal machine learning in production.

Experiments say what a change does on average. The next question is for whom. The Island's marketplace has a coupon for 30 percent of its fifty thousand customers. It raises most customers' chance of buying a little, but for 15 percent it only costs money: they would have bought anyway. The usual targeting rule sends coupons to the customers most likely to buy. Here that yields -0.7 purchases per hundred coupons, worse than sending them at random, +6.1, because the likeliest buyers are exactly the ones who need no coupon. Target by the effect instead, estimated from an experiment by an uplift model, and the coupons yield +12.2, close to the +12.9 a planner who knew everyone's true effect would get. This is where machine learning met causal inference in industry: causal forests and their relatives estimate how an effect varies, the methods Susan Athey and Guido Imbens brought from statistics into economics.

How is such a model judged? Not by how well it predicts purchases, but by what its ranking is worth. Give coupons in order of estimated effect, and add up the extra purchases. Against it, the same number given at random. The curve rises steeply, flattens, and turns down at the end, where the coupons go to the customers they harm. The area between the two curves, measured on customers held out of the training, is the model's score: the economics of targeting, put in a single number.

The hardest question is the long run. Experiments last weeks; the decisions are about years. The Island tests a month-long discount. Orders in the first month rise by 41 percent: a triumph, if the test stops there. But some customers learn to wait for the next discount, and their visits in the second month fall. The year's orders actually fall, by 3.1 percent. Susan Athey, Raj Chetty, Guido Imbens and Hyunseung Kang proposed the surrogate index: in last year's data, learn how the year's orders depend on the first two months' behaviour, then apply that relation to the experiment's two arms after eight weeks. The index predicts -3.4 percent, close to the truth of -3.1, ten months early. It works only if the short-run measures carry the whole effect of the treatment on the long run; a discount that also changed something the surrogates miss would fool it.
Gig: Ride-hailing drivers choose their own hours, minute by minute. What is that worth to them? Take one Island driver. Each bar is what it would take to get them on the road in that hour: low when the children are at school, high at dinner time, different every day. The app pays twenty dollars an hour. A flexible driver drives exactly the green hours, when the pay beats the alternative, and earns the gap. A taxi company would offer a fixed eight-hour shift instead: the best block of eight hours, taken whole, bad hours included, or not at all. Across five thousand Island drivers, the surplus from driving is 54 dollars a day with flexible hours and 16 with shifts. Flexibility is worth 3.3 times what the shift leaves, and only 44 percent of these drivers would take a shift at all.

The platform's own data show what drivers do. M. Keith Chen, Judith Chevalier, Peter Rossi and Emily Oehlsen used drivers' hour-by-hour choices to recover their reservation wages, as the Island does. They found that drivers earn more than twice the surplus they would in less flexible arrangements. Most drive part time, around other work and family, and their hours move with the pay. Cody Cook, Rebecca Diamond, Jonathan Hall, John List and Paul Oyer found that among over a million drivers men earned about seven percent more an hour, on a platform whose pay formula never looks at gender. The gap came from experience, from where and when they drove, and from driving faster. What flexibility costs is everything a job usually carries: pay for waiting, sick pay, a pension. The risk sits with the driver.

And then there is the law. Is a driver an employee? In 2019 California passed a law whose test would treat most such workers as employees. In 2020 its voters passed Proposition twenty-two, exempting app-based drivers, with an earnings floor and some benefits instead. In 2021 Britain's Supreme Court ruled that Uber's drivers are workers, entitled to the minimum wage and holiday pay. The economist's question is the trade the chapter has measured: what employment's protections cost in flexibility, and who ends up paying, riders through fares, drivers through fewer hours, or the platform through its margin.
Data: Chapter twelve. Data, attention and free goods.

A search engine charges its users nothing, so it adds nothing to their measured spending, and almost nothing to GDP. What is it worth? Ask what it would take to give it up. Four thousand Island users are each offered a random sum to go without search for a year, and the offer is real: accept it and the search is switched off. The share who accept rises with the offer. Fit a logit in the log of the offer, and half accept at 14,171 dollars: the median user values free search at about that much a year. The value the Island planted was 15,000.

Erik Brynjolfsson, Avinash Collis and Felix Eggers asked Americans this question at scale. The median user would give up search engines for a year only for about seventeen and a half thousand dollars, email for about eight thousand four hundred, and digital maps for about three thousand six hundred. To give up Facebook for a month, the median was about forty-eight dollars. None of this value appears in GDP, which measures what is paid, so Brynjolfsson and his colleagues propose measuring the welfare from free goods alongside it.

Free is not quite free. The user pays with attention and data, which the platform sells to advertisers: Part forty-four's two-sided market, with the user's information as an input. How much do people mind? Susan Athey, Christian Catalini and Catherine Tucker found that students who said they cared about privacy still handed over their friends' email addresses for a free pizza: stated preferences and choices part company, as they did in Part sixty's surveys. What data is worth to the platform is how much better it targets; to the user, the risk of what it reveals; the two are rarely measured together. And the rules, consent, limits on tracking, the right to take your data elsewhere, each change what this market can price.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: surge elasticities and the return on search ads.

This part opens two Dials and returns to a third. The first: how much riders' bookings fall when the fare rises. Cohen and his co-authors, over the whole sample: minus 0.55. In Los Angeles, minus 0.33, on weekend days minus 0.66, on weekdays outside the rush hours minus 0.46. The Island's riders, minus 0.59, planted to sit inside that range. The status: it depends on the setting, but every estimate is well below one in size. Demand for a ride on a busy night is inelastic, which is why surge clears the market mainly by bringing out drivers, and why riders keep so much surplus.

The second: the return on search advertising, in extra revenue per dollar, less the dollar. eBay's experiment: minus 0.63, with an interval that stays below zero. The same data without the experiment: plus 16.3. The Island's experiment and its regression repeat the pattern, by construction: the truth was planted below zero. The status is contested, and for an unusual reason. The two kinds of estimate do not merely differ in size; they differ in sign. Ads that reach new customers can pay; ads shown to people already on their way to buy cannot, and only an experiment tells the two apart.

And the Dial from Part sixteen returns, with chapter six's auctions behind it: what a reserve price adds to an ad auction's revenue. Ostrovsky and Schwarz's experiment at Yahoo!, at fixed search volumes: plus 2.7 percent overall, minus 2.2 percent on keywords searched fewer than ten times a day, and plus 3.3 percent on the busy ones. The theory's reserve raises revenue where bidders were many, and cost it where they were few, by driving some of them away: a lesson the static theory, which holds the bidders fixed, does not teach.
Frontier: Chapter fifteen. Frontier: markets of agents.

The frontier is a marketplace where software shops and sells on people's behalf. Suppose prices for the same thing spread from ten dollars to twenty. A person checks a couple of sellers and pays, on average, 13.33. An agent that checks twenty pays 10.48. But that holds the sellers still, and they would not stay still. When searching is free, the spread of prices that made it worth searching shrinks, as the economics of search predicts; the gains go to buyers through competition, not through bargains. And the sellers will have agents too, setting prices by algorithms that, as Part sixty showed, can learn not to compete. Who wins a market of agents depends on the rules the platform writes for them.

What remains open? Recommendation and welfare. A feed tuned for engagement is not a feed tuned for well-being. Hunt Allcott, Luca Braghieri, Sarah Eichmeyer and Matthew Gentzkow paid people to deactivate Facebook for four weeks before the 2018 American elections: they spent the time offline and with friends, reported somewhat higher well-being, and followed the news less. Platforms for agents: who pays the commission, and what does a ranking mean, when the buyer is a program? Experiments among agents: when every user's agent reacts to every test, chapter nine's interference is everywhere. And the hardest of all, which runs through the whole part: platforms measure what users do, and the economist's question is whether they are better off.
